      <content name="title"><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Nose</span></span> Injuries and Disorders</content>

      <content name="altTitle"><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Nasal</span></span> Disorders</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Nosebleed</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">nose</span></span> is important to your health. It filters the air you breathe, removing dust, germs, and irritants. It warms and moistens the air to keep your lungs and tubes that lead to them from drying out. Your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">nose</span></span> also contains the nerve cells that help your sense of smell. When there is a problem with your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">nose</span></span>, your whole body can suffer. For example, the stuffy <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">nose</span></span> of the common cold can make it hard for you to breathe, sleep, or get comfortable. </p><p>Many problems besides the common cold can affect the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">nose</span></span>. They include:</p><ul><li>	Deviated septum - a shifting of the wall that divides the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">nasal</span></span> cavity into halves</li><li>	<span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Nasal</span></span> <span class="qt2">polyps</span> - soft growths that develop on the lining of your <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">nose</span></span> or sinuses</li><li>	Nosebleeds </li><li>	Rhinitis - inflammation of the <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">nose</span></span> and sinuses sometimes caused by allergies. The main symptom is a runny <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">nose</span></span>.</li><li><span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">Nasal</span></span> fractures, also known as a broken <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">nose</span></span></li></ul></content>

    <document rank="1" url="https://medlineplus.gov/benigntumors.html">
      <content name="title">Benign Tumors</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Adenoma</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Hemangioma</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Tumors, Benign</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Benign neoplasms</content>
      <content name="altTitle">Noncancerous tumors</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Tumors are abnormal growths in your body. They can be either benign or malignant. Benign tumors aren't cancer. Malignant ones are. Benign tumors grow only in one place. They cannot spread or invade other parts of your body. Even so, they can be dangerous if they press on vital organs, such as your brain.</p><p>Tumors are made up of extra cells. Normally, cells grow and divide to form new cells as your body needs them. When cells grow old, they die, and new cells take their place. Sometimes, this process goes wrong. New cells form when your body does not need them, and old cells do not die when they should. These extra cells can divide without stopping and may form a tumor.</p><p>Treatment often involves surgery. Benign tumors usually don't grow back.</p><p>NIH: National Cancer Institute</p></content>

    <document rank="2" url="https://medlineplus.gov/eardisorders.html">
      <content name="title">Ear Disorders</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary">What is an ear disorder?<p>An ear disorder is any condition that changes or harms the shape or structure of your ear. This can include abnormal ear shapes you're born with, injuries that change your ear's shape, and a growth on or in the ear.</p><p>Your ear has three main parts, and each one plays a different role in helping you hear:</p><ul><li>Outer ear. The part you see and the ear canal. It catches sound and sends them to your eardrum.</li><li>Middle ear. When sound reaches your eardrum, it vibrates. These vibrations move through three small bones, called ossicles, that carry them further into your ear.</li><li>Inner ear. Changes vibrations into nerve signals your brain understands as sound. It also helps you keep your balance.</li></ul><p>Many conditions may affect your hearing or balance:</p><ul><li>Ear infections, the most common illness in infants and young children</li><li>Tinnitus, a ringing or roaring in your ears</li><li>Meniere's disease, which may be caused by fluid problems in your inner ear</li><li>Ear barotrauma, an ear injury from sudden air or water pressure changes</li></ul><p>Some of these conditions can also lead to hearing disorders and deafness.</p>What causes ear disorders?<p>Ear disorders may be caused by:</p><ul><li>Abnormal ear shapes you're born with, like microtia and anotia, which usually have no known cause. Sometimes they're linked to genes or certain medicines taken during pregnancy.</li><li>Injury from hits, cuts, or bites can damage the ear.</li><li>Growths that form after an injury, piercing, repeated cold water exposure, or years in the sun.</li><li>Infections, like perichondritis, which often start from a cut or piercing.</li><li>Bone growth in the middle ear, called otosclerosis, which can run in families.</li></ul>What are the symptoms of ear disorders?<p>Sometimes the only sign of an ear disorder is how your ear looks. Other symptoms may include:</p><ul><li>Changes in the size or shape of your ear</li><li>Swelling, redness, or growths</li><li>Pain or tenderness</li><li>Scarring or changes in skin color</li><li>Cuts or holes in the ear or eardrum</li><li>Slow hearing loss, in some cases</li></ul>How are ear disorders diagnosed?<p>To find out if you have an ear disorder, your health care provider may:</p><ul><li>Do a physical exam</li><li>Look inside your ear with a lighted tool called an otoscope</li><li>Order [imaging tests] to see bones or tissue more clearly</li><li>Test your hearing</li><li>Order a biopsy, to check if a growth is cancer</li></ul><p>Sometimes, your provider may refer you to a doctor who specializes in care of the ear, <span class="qt0"><span class="qt1">nose</span></span>, and throat.</p>How are ear disorders treated?<p>Treatment for an ear disorder depends on the cause. Some may be treated with medicine. Others may need surgery to change the shape of the ear or remove a growth. If the disorder affects your hearing, you may need a hearing aid.</p>Can ear disorders be prevented?<p>Most ear disorders that you are born with can't be prevented. But you can help to prevent some ear disorders by:</p><ul><li>Wearing head protection during sports</li><li>Treating cuts and injuries</li><li>Caring for new piercings</li><li>Protecting your ears from cold water and the sun</li></ul></content>

    <document rank="3" url="https://medlineplus.gov/biopsy.html">
      <content name="title">Biopsy</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>A biopsy is a procedure that removes cells or tissue from your body.  A doctor called a pathologist looks at the cells or tissue under a microscope to check for damage or disease. The pathologist may also do other tests on it.</p><p>Biopsies can be done on all parts of the body. In most cases, a biopsy is the only test that can tell for sure if a suspicious area is cancer.  But biopsies are performed for many other reasons too.</p><p>There are different types of biopsies. A needle biopsy removes tissue with a needle passed through your skin to the site of the problem. Other kinds of biopsies may require surgery.</p></content>

    <document rank="4" url="https://medlineplus.gov/endoscopy.html">
      <content name="title">Endoscopy</content>
      <content name="organizationName">National Library of Medicine</content>
      <content name="FullSummary"><p>Endoscopy is a procedure that lets your doctor look inside your body. It uses an instrument called an endoscope, or scope for short.  Scopes have a tiny camera attached to a long, thin tube. The doctor moves it through a body passageway or opening to see inside an organ. Sometimes scopes are used for surgery, such as for removing <span class="qt2">polyps</span> from the colon.</p><p>There are many different kinds of endoscopy. Here are the names of some of them and where they look.:</p><ul><li>Arthroscopy: joints</li><li>Bronchoscopy: lungs</li><li>Colonoscopy and sigmoidoscopy: large intestine</li><li>Cystoscopy and ureteroscopy: urinary system</li><li>Laparoscopy: abdomen or pelvis</li><li>Upper gastrointestinal endoscopy: esophagus and stomach </li></ul></content>
